faq.a: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is the most frequent cause of androgen excess and virilization in women of reproductive age.
faq.q: What is the most common cause of virilization?

faq.a: Many symptoms, like hirsutism and acne, can be managed and improved with treatment. However, some changes like voice deepening or clitoromegaly may be irreversible.

A detailed history and physical exam are crucial. Look for rapid onset, severe symptoms, or palpable masses. If available, basic tests like a pregnancy test and glucose can help. Referral may be necessary.
faq.q: What if I don't have access to hormone tests?

exam: A 25-year-old woman presents with a 1-year history of increasing facial hair, acne, and irregular periods. Her voice has deepened slightly. What is your differential diagnosis, and what is the most likely diagnosis in a low-resource setting? — PCOS is most common; consider adrenal tumors, CAH, exogenous androgens.

How would you differentiate between an ovarian and an adrenal cause of virilization based on initial investigations? — Elevated testosterone with normal or mildly elevated DHEAS suggests an ovarian source. Markedly elevated DHEAS strongly suggests an adrenal source.

A patient has clitoromegaly and a palpable abdominal mass. What are your immediate concerns and next steps? — High suspicion for an androgen-secreting tumor (ovarian or adrenal). Urgent imaging and hormonal workup are needed.

You suspect Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH) in a woman with virilization. What is the key diagnostic test, and what result confirms the diagnosis? — 17-hydroxyprogesterone. Elevated levels, especially after ACTH stimulation, confirm CAH.

Why is spironolactone often used in managing virilization, and what are its potential side effects? — It's an anti-androgen and potassium-sparing diuretic. Side effects include hyperkalemia, dizziness, and menstrual irregularities.

A patient with virilization has normal testosterone and DHEAS levels. What other causes should you consider? — Idiopathic hirsutism, certain medications (e.g., anabolic steroids), or rare conditions affecting androgen receptors.
ai.title: Virilization in Women
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Virilization refers to the development of male physical characteristics in females. It is most commonly caused by excess androgens, often from adrenal or ovarian sources. Evaluation involves history, physical exam, and hormonal testing to identify the underlying cause.

sections.p: Virilization is the appearance of physical characteristics typically associated with males in females. This occurs due to excessive exposure to androgens (male sex hormones). The severity and speed of onset can vary, impacting reproductive health, fertility, and psychological well-being.

Androgens, primarily testosterone, are responsible for male secondary sexual characteristics. In females, ovaries and adrenal glands produce small amounts of androgens. When these glands produce excess androgens, or when there is increased sensitivity to androgens, virilization can occur.

b: Hirsutism: excess coarse hair growth in a male pattern (face, chest, back).
Acne: severe or persistent acne.
Alopecia: male-pattern hair loss on the scalp.
Clitoromegaly: enlargement of the clitoris.
Deepening of the voice.
Increased muscle mass.
Decreased breast size.
Menstrual irregularities or amenorrhea.
sections.p: Virilization in women is a sign of an underlying endocrine disorder. It can affect fertility, menstrual cycles, and self-image. Prompt diagnosis and management are crucial to address the cause and prevent further progression.

b: Ovarian causes: Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS) is the most common. Ovarian tumors (rare).
Adrenal causes: Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH), adrenal tumors (rare), Cushing's syndrome.
Exogenous sources: Anabolic steroid use, certain medications.
Idiopathic: In some cases, no clear cause is found.
sections.p: Causes are broadly categorized by the source of excess androgens:

t.b: To assess the level of male hormones. Elevated levels suggest an androgen-producing tumor or other significant androgen excess.
To evaluate adrenal androgen production. Markedly elevated levels often point to an adrenal source, such as an adrenal tumor.
Screening test for Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia (CAH). Elevated levels, especially after ACTH stimulation, confirm CAH.
To rule out a prolactinoma, which can cause menstrual irregularities and sometimes mild virilization.
To assess the hypothalamic-pituitary-ovarian axis, especially useful in diagnosing PCOS.
To visualize ovaries for signs of PCOS (polycystic morphology, increased stroma) or ovarian tumors.
To evaluate adrenal glands for tumors or hyperplasia if DHEAS is significantly elevated.

b: Address the underlying cause: surgery for tumors, specific medical therapy for CAH or Cushing's.
Anti-androgens: Medications like spironolactone or cyproterone acetate block androgen action.
Oral contraceptives: Can suppress ovarian androgen production and regulate menses.
Lifestyle: Weight loss if obese (especially in PCOS), diet modification.
Cosmetic treatments: For hirsutism and alopecia, such as laser hair removal or topical treatments.
sections.p: Management focuses on treating the underlying cause and managing symptoms. Lifestyle modifications and medications are key.

b: Rapid onset of virilizing symptoms.
Significant clitoromegaly.
Palpable ovarian or adrenal mass.
Severe hormonal abnormalities suggesting malignancy.
A thorough menstrual history is vital: regularity, duration, and any recent changes.
Careful examination for signs of androgen excess: Ferriman-Gallwey score for hirsutism, assess clitoris size, voice changes, and hair loss pattern.
Palpate abdomen and flanks for masses.
Consider the patient's age and reproductive status when interpreting findings.
Confusing hirsutism (excess hair growth) with hypertrichosis (generalized excess hair growth).
Attributing all menstrual irregularities to PCOS without considering other causes.
Delaying investigation of virilization, especially if symptoms are severe or rapidly progressive.
Not considering exogenous androgen use as a cause.
